elements.name: Monitor
elements.what: A dedicated component monitors the health of other parts of the system (processors, processes, I/O, memory) and coordinates the other fault-detection tactics.
elements.problem: Faults must be observed by some part of the system before any repair can begin; a system needs a designated observer to detect failures or congestion, e.g. denial-of-service conditions.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Ping/Echo
elements.what: Nodes exchange asynchronous request/response message pairs to determine reachability and round-trip delay, with a time threshold before the pinged component is declared failed.
elements.problem: A monitor must determine whether a remote component is alive and reachable over a network path, and how long the path takes.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Heartbeat
elements.what: A monitored component periodically emits a message to (or resets a watchdog timer in) a system monitor, so that the absence of the heartbeat signals failure.
elements.problem: Failure of a component must be detected without the monitor having to actively probe it; the component itself takes the initiative to demonstrate liveness.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Timestamp
elements.what: Assign the state of a local clock (or a sequence number) to events immediately after they occur so that incorrect event ordering can be detected.
elements.problem: In distributed message-passing systems, events may arrive or be processed out of order and local clocks may be inconsistent across processors.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Condition Monitoring
elements.what: Check conditions in a process or device, or validate assumptions made during design (e.g. by computing checksums), to prevent the system from producing faulty behavior.
elements.problem: A system can drift outside its assumed operating conditions without any single operation failing; the monitor itself must be simple enough not to introduce new faults.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Sanity Checking
elements.what: Check the validity or reasonableness of a component's specific operations or outputs, typically at interfaces, based on knowledge of the internal design, system state, or the nature of the information.
elements.problem: A component can produce syntactically valid but semantically implausible results; examining specific information flows catches such faults early.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Voting
elements.what: Compare computational results from multiple sources that should produce the same result and decide which to use when they differ, using simple, heavily reviewed voting logic.
elements.problem: A single component's output cannot be trusted in the presence of hardware or software faults; multiple evaluable sources plus a highly reliable voter allow faulty results to be outvoted.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Replication
elements.what: Provide multiple identical copies of a component so their results can be voted on or a copy can take over; effective against random hardware faults.
elements.problem: Random hardware failures can silently corrupt a single component's behavior; pure replication offers no diversity, so it does not protect against design or implementation faults.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Functional Redundancy
elements.what: Provide redundant components that are diversely designed and implemented but must produce the same output for the same input.
elements.problem: Common-mode failures defeat identical replicas because copies sharing an implementation fail together; diversity in the redundancy addresses systematic design faults, at higher development and verification cost.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Analytic Redundancy
elements.what: Provide redundant components that are diverse not only internally but also in their inputs and outputs (e.g. computing aircraft altitude by barometric pressure, radar, and geometry), with a sophisticated blending/voting mechanism.
elements.problem: Specification errors defeat functionally redundant components built to the same specification; independent requirement specifications and diverse input sources tolerate them, and help when some inputs are intermittently unavailable.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Exception Detection
elements.what: Detect system conditions that alter the normal flow of execution, refined by the book into system exceptions, parameter fence, parameter typing, and timeout.
elements.problem: Faults such as divide-by-zero, bus/address faults, illegal instructions, or violated timing constraints must be turned into detectable events rather than silent corruption.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Parameter Fence
elements.what: Place a known data pattern immediately after any variable-length parameters of an object so that overwrites of that memory can be detected at runtime.
elements.problem: Buffer overruns into memory allocated for variable-length parameters are otherwise silent until they corrupt unrelated state.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)
elements.borderline: Reads as an implementation-level guard mechanism (kin to design-realm canaries/guard bytes), but bck names it explicitly as an availability sub-tactic; kept per over-inclusion rule.

elements.name: Parameter Typing
elements.what: Use a base class defining functions to add, find, and iterate over type-length-value (TLV) message parameters so that sender and receiver agree on content types and disagreements are detected.
elements.problem: Untyped message payloads let sender and receiver silently disagree about the meaning of bytes on the wire.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)
elements.borderline: Implementation-flavored like parameter fence, but named as an availability sub-tactic in bck; kept per over-inclusion rule.

elements.name: Timeout
elements.what: A component raises an exception when it detects that it or another component has failed to meet its timing constraints, e.g. when a response takes longer than a set bound.
elements.problem: Hung or slow components would otherwise block their clients indefinitely; violated time constraints must become detectable events.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Self-Test
elements.what: A component or subsystem runs procedures to test itself for correct operation, initiated by itself or invoked periodically by the system monitor.
elements.problem: Latent faults in a component may not manifest during normal operation until they matter; proactive self-exercise surfaces them early.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Redundant Spare
elements.what: Configure one or more spare components that can step in and take over when an active component fails; hot/warm/cold variants differ in how current the spare's state is at takeover.
elements.problem: A failed active component must be replaced quickly to keep the service available; the trade-off is between resource cost of keeping spares synchronized and recovery time.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Rollback
elements.what: On detecting a failure, revert the system to a previously saved known-good state (the rollback line), captured as checkpoints, and resume execution from there.
elements.problem: A failure can leave state corrupted; recovery requires a consistent earlier state to return to, often combined with transactions and redundant spares.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Exception Handling
elements.what: After an exception is detected, handle it using mechanisms ranging from function return codes to exception classes carrying name, origin, and cause, so the fault can be masked or repaired.
elements.problem: Simply crashing on a detected exception is unacceptable for availability; the system needs structured information and a place to act on it.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Software Upgrade
elements.what: Upgrade executable code images in service, without affecting the running service, via function patches, class patches, or hitless in-service software upgrade built on redundant spares.
elements.problem: Deploying fixes and features to systems that must not stop requires replacing code while it runs.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Retry
elements.what: Assume the fault that caused a failure is transient and retry the operation, with a limit on the number of attempts before declaring a permanent failure.
elements.problem: In networks and server farms transient failures are expected and common; treating every failure as permanent wastes the chance of cheap recovery.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Ignore Faulty Behavior
elements.what: Ignore messages from a particular source once they are determined to be spurious, e.g. messages from a sensor known to have failed.
elements.problem: A faulty component can flood the system with bogus events; continuing to act on them propagates the fault.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Degradation
elements.what: In the presence of component failures, maintain the most critical system functions while dropping or substituting less critical ones in a planned, deliberate, safe way.
elements.problem: Individual component failures should reduce system functionality gracefully rather than cause total collapse; e.g. a navigation system falling back to dead reckoning in a tunnel.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Reconfiguration
elements.what: Recover from failure by reassigning responsibilities — remapping the logical architecture onto the (possibly limited) resources or components still functioning — while preserving as much functionality as possible.
elements.problem: After failures the remaining resources differ from the planned deployment; the system must keep operating on what is left, possibly combined with degradation.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Shadow
elements.what: Run a previously failed or freshly upgraded component in shadow mode for a predefined period, monitoring its behavior and letting it repopulate state before restoring it to an active role.
elements.problem: Reintroducing a repaired component directly into active service risks reintroducing the fault; its correctness must be demonstrated first.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: State Resynchronization
elements.what: Restore and verify state consistency between active and standby components, either naturally under active redundancy (with periodic comparison via checksums or message digests) or by periodic state transfer/checkpointing under passive redundancy.
elements.problem: A reintroduced or standby component must have state consistent with the active one before it can safely take over.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Escalating Restart
elements.what: Recover by restarting components at progressively coarser granularity levels (e.g. child threads only, then unprotected memory, then all memory, then full image reload), choosing the least disruptive level that clears the fault.
elements.problem: A full restart is maximally disruptive; matching the restart granularity to the fault minimizes the impact on service, supporting graceful degradation.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Non-Stop Forwarding
elements.what: Split functionality into a control/management plane and a data plane so that when the control plane fails, the data plane keeps forwarding along known routes while routing information is rebuilt and validated.
elements.problem: In router-like systems, supervisory failure should not stop the ongoing data-moving work; the concept originates in router design.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Removal from Service
elements.what: Temporarily place a system component out of service and reset it to scrub latent faults (memory leaks, fragmentation, soft errors) before they accumulate into failures.
elements.problem: Latent faults accumulate during long operation; proactive resets prevent them from ever affecting service.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Transactions
elements.what: Use transaction semantics (ACID properties, most commonly implemented via two-phase commit) to bundle state updates exchanged between distributed components so they are atomic, consistent, isolated, and durable.
elements.problem: Race conditions from concurrent updates to the same data, and partial failures mid-update, would otherwise leave inconsistent state.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Predictive Model
elements.what: Combine a model with monitoring to predict, from operational metrics (session establishment rates, threshold crossings, process-state and queue-length statistics), that a fault or unsafe condition is approaching, and take corrective action early.
elements.problem: Waiting for faults to occur before reacting is too late for high-availability and safety-critical operation; early warning enables preemptive correction.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Exception Prevention
elements.what: Employ techniques that keep exceptions from arising at all — error-correcting codes, abstract data types such as smart pointers, and wrappers that preclude dangling pointers or semaphore access violations.
elements.problem: Whole fault classes (resource leaks, out-of-bounds access) can be excluded by construction more cheaply than detecting and recovering from them.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Increase Competence Set
elements.what: Design a component to handle more cases — states that would otherwise be faults — as part of its normal operation, e.g. waiting or returning gracefully when a resource is blocked instead of throwing.
elements.problem: A component throws an exception when it finds itself outside the set of states it is competent to handle; enlarging that set converts faults into handled situations.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Scale Rollouts
elements.what: Deploy a new version of a service gradually to controlled subsets of the user population rather than to everyone at once, monitoring effects and rolling back if needed; blue/green deployment and rolling upgrade are pattern realizations.
elements.problem: Deploying a defective service to all users maximizes damage; incremental exposure requires an architectural mechanism outside the service that routes each user's requests to the new or old version.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Rollback (Deployment)
elements.what: Revert a defective or disappointing deployment to its prior state, tracking or being able to reverse the coordinated updates to multiple services and their data, ideally fully automatically.
elements.problem: A deployment may involve many coordinated service and data updates; discovering a defect after release requires undoing all of them safely. Distinct mechanism from the availability Rollback tactic, which reverts runtime state to a checkpoint.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Script Deployment Commands
elements.what: Capture the many precisely ordered, coordinated deployment steps as scripts that are treated like code — documented, reviewed, tested, version-controlled — and executed by a script engine.
elements.problem: Complex manual deployments are slow and error-prone; automation removes human error and makes deployments repeatable.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Manage Service Interactions
elements.what: Allow multiple versions of system services to be deployed and executed simultaneously, with client requests routed to any version, coordinating inter-service interactions to proactively avoid version incompatibilities.
elements.problem: Simultaneously running old and new versions avoids fully duplicating resources during upgrade but introduces version-compatibility hazards that must be managed.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Package Dependencies
elements.what: Package an element together with its dependencies (libraries, OS version, utility containers) — via containers, pods, or virtual machines — so they deploy together and dependency versions stay consistent from development to production.
elements.problem: An element that behaves correctly in development can fail in production when the surrounding dependency versions differ.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Feature Toggle
elements.what: Integrate a runtime 'kill switch' for new features so a deployed feature can be automatically disabled without initiating a new deployment.
elements.problem: Even fully tested features can misbehave after deployment; controlling them without the cost and risk of redeploying requires a toggle mechanism in the architecture.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Metering
elements.what: Collect data about the energy consumption of computing resources in near real time via a sensor infrastructure — from data-center meters down to metered rack PDUs, ASICs, or battery management systems.
elements.problem: Energy cannot be managed without being measured; different granularities of measurement need different instrumentation.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Static Classification
elements.what: Estimate energy consumption by cataloging the computing resources used and their known static energy characteristics (from benchmarks or manufacturer specifications), e.g. energy per disk read.
elements.problem: Real-time energy data collection is sometimes impossible (e.g. on external cloud services); reference models substitute for measurement.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Dynamic Classification
elements.what: Estimate energy consumption with a dynamic model — a table lookup, a regression over past executions, or a simulation — that accounts for transient conditions such as workload.
elements.problem: Static energy models are insufficient when consumption depends heavily on runtime conditions.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Reduce Usage
elements.what: Reduce energy use by device-level actions (lower refresh rate, dim display), removing or deactivating unneeded resources (spin down disks, power off CPUs/servers, reduce clock rate), consolidating VMs onto fewer physical servers, or offloading computation to the cloud.
elements.problem: Resources kept powered beyond demand waste energy; usage must track need.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Encapsulate
elements.what: Introduce an explicit interface to an element and hide its internals so that other elements depend only on the interface, reducing the strength of coupling and the syntactic/semantic distance to be bridged.
elements.problem: Direct dependence on an element's internals means every internal change and every integration must confront those internals; an interface localizes the dependency.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Use an Intermediary
elements.what: Break a dependency between elements by interposing an intermediary (broker, publish-subscribe bus, name server, etc.) that manages the interaction on their behalf.
elements.problem: Direct dependencies between many elements multiply coupling and integration effort; an intermediary centralizes and standardizes the interaction, at some performance cost.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Restrict Communication Paths
elements.what: Restrict the set of elements with which a given element can communicate, so the number of potential interaction points that must be understood and integrated stays small.
elements.problem: Unrestricted many-to-many communication makes the integration surface of each element grow with the system; deliberate path restriction contains it.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Adhere to Standards
elements.what: Conform to published interface, protocol, and data standards so that elements built independently can interoperate with less adaptation.
elements.problem: Idiosyncratic interfaces force per-pair integration work; standardization lets the ecosystem amortize it.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Abstract Common Services
elements.what: Where elements provide similar services, factor the similarity into a single more general/abstract service used by all, hiding the specifics of the variants.
elements.problem: Duplicate similar services multiply both modification cost (each copy changes) and integration surface; one abstraction localizes both.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Discover
elements.what: Match service requests to service providers at runtime through a discovery service, enabling identification and remote invocation of providers that were not bound at build time; in the energy context, requests can be annotated so providers are selected by energy characteristics.
elements.problem: Statically bound providers cannot be swapped or selected by runtime criteria (location, version, energy cost); a discovery mechanism defers and mediates the binding.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Tailor Interface
elements.what: Add capabilities to or hide capabilities of an interface without changing the underlying implementation — e.g. adding buffering, data transformation, or masking functions (adapter/decorator-like mechanisms at the architectural boundary).
elements.problem: Independently developed components rarely present exactly the interfaces their integrators need; adapting at the interface avoids modifying either side.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Configure Behavior
elements.what: Build components so their behavior can be configured — during build, deployment/startup, or runtime — to operate in the modes an integrating system expects.
elements.problem: A component with a single fixed behavior fits only one integration context; configurability lets one implementation satisfy many.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Orchestrate
elements.what: Introduce a control mechanism (e.g. an orchestration engine or workflow controller) that coordinates, sequences, and invokes otherwise independent services so they work together.
elements.problem: Independently developed services have no shared control flow; centralizing coordination keeps the integration logic out of the services themselves.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Manage Resources (Integrability)
elements.what: Interpose an explicit resource manager that mediates access to shared computing resources (memory, threads, hardware devices) so independently developed components can share them safely.
elements.problem: Components that each assume exclusive resource ownership conflict when integrated; a mediator arbitrates. (Named 'Manage Resources' in bck's integrability chapter; not to be confused with the performance category of the same name.)
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Split Module
elements.what: Refactor a module whose responsibilities are not cohesive into several modules that are each individually cohesive — not an arbitrary bisection, but a principled separation of responsibilities.
elements.problem: When one module carries unrelated responsibilities, changes to any of them cost as much as changing all; splitting reduces the average cost of future change.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Redistribute Responsibilities
elements.what: Move similar responsibilities scattered across several modules into one module (existing or new), guided by change scenarios showing which responsibilities move together.
elements.problem: When one likely change touches many modules, or a module contains parts untouched by any scenario, responsibilities are misallocated and change cost multiplies.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Restrict Dependencies
elements.what: Restrict which modules a given module may interact with or depend on, in practice via interface visibility and authorization; seen in layered architectures (a layer may use only lower layers) and wrappers (outsiders see only the wrapper).
elements.problem: Unconstrained dependency graphs let changes ripple arbitrarily; restricting the allowed edges bounds the ripple. Sibling of the integrability tactic Restrict Communication Paths, kept separate as bck names both.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Defer Binding
elements.what: Bind values and choices as late in the life cycle as cost-effective: at compile/build time (component replacement, compile-time parameterization, aspects), at deployment/startup (configuration-time binding, resource files), or at runtime (discovery, interpreted parameters, shared repositories, polymorphism).
elements.problem: Human-mediated change is costly and error-prone; building in flexibility lets computers effect the change, trading up-front mechanism cost against per-change cost and enabling change by non-developers ('externalizing' change).
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Manage Event Arrival
elements.what: Control the arrival rate of events from external systems, canonically by setting a service level agreement that fixes the maximum event rate the system will support, constraining both system and clients.
elements.problem: Demand beyond the sustainable arrival rate degrades everyone's response time; capping arrivals makes load explicit and pushes overflow to additional instances.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Manage Sampling Rate
elements.what: Reduce (possibly dynamically) the frequency at which environmental input is sampled — sensor data rates, video frames per second — trading fidelity for predictable latency.
elements.problem: When the system cannot keep up with the incoming data stream, lower-fidelity but stable processing may beat unstable latency; common in signal-processing systems.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Limit Event Response
elements.what: Process events only up to a set maximum rate, queueing or deliberately dropping events that arrive faster, triggered by queue size, processor utilization, or SLA violation.
elements.problem: Bursts beyond processing capacity force a policy choice: guarantee no loss (size queues for the worst case) or drop events (and decide whether to log or notify).
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Prioritize Events
elements.what: Impose a priority scheme ordering events by importance of servicing them, so that under resource pressure low-priority events may be ignored at minimal cost.
elements.problem: Not all events are equally important (a fire alarm vs. a room-temperature notice); treating them uniformly wastes resources on the unimportant under load.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Reduce Computational Overhead
elements.what: Reduce the work spent per event by removing costly indirection (while ideally preserving encapsulation through code optimization or proxy-established direct communication), co-locating communicating components (same processor, same runtime, same rack), and periodically cleaning inefficient-grown resources such as hash tables and virtual memory maps.
elements.problem: Intermediaries and separation of concerns — valuable for modifiability — add per-event processing and communication cost; this is the classic modifiability/performance trade-off.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Bound Execution Times
elements.what: Place a limit on how much execution time is used to respond to an event — e.g. bounding iteration counts in data-dependent iterative algorithms — trading computational accuracy for bounded latency.
elements.problem: Unbounded computations make response time unpredictable; often paired with Manage Sampling Rate, and requires assessing whether the less-accurate result is good enough.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Increase Resource Usage Efficiency
elements.what: Improve the efficiency of the algorithms used in critical areas to decrease latency and improve throughput and resource consumption.
elements.problem: Inefficient critical-path algorithms consume resources that better algorithms would free; 'optimizing the code' is one tactic among many, not the only lever.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Increase Resources
elements.what: Add or upgrade resources — faster processors, additional processors, more memory, faster networks — to improve performance.
elements.problem: When demand cannot be reduced, capacity must grow; despite its cost, adding resources is often the cheapest immediate route to better performance.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Introduce Concurrency
elements.what: Process requests in parallel — different event streams on different threads, or additional threads for different activity sets — to reduce blocked time, then choose a scheduling policy via Schedule Resources.
elements.problem: Serialized processing leaves requests blocked behind one another even when independent; concurrency reclaims that waiting time.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Maintain Multiple Copies of Computations
elements.what: Run multiple replicas of a computation (replicated services in a microservice architecture, replicated web servers in a pool) with a load balancer assigning new work among them.
elements.problem: Funneling all service requests through a single instance creates contention; replicas spread the load.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Maintain Multiple Copies of Data
elements.what: Keep copies of data — replication (separate identical copies to reduce contention) or caching (copies, possibly subsets, on storage with different access speeds, possibly predictively prefetched) — accepting the burden of keeping copies consistent.
elements.problem: Simultaneous access to one copy of data creates contention, and distant/slow storage adds latency; copies trade consistency-maintenance work for reduced contention and faster access.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Bound Queue Sizes
elements.what: Control the maximum number of queued arrivals, and thereby the resources used to process them, with an explicit policy for what happens when queues overflow.
elements.problem: Unbounded queues consume unbounded resources and hide overload; bounding them forces a deliberate overflow/loss policy, usually paired with Limit Event Response.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Schedule Resources
elements.what: When resources (processors, buffers, networks) are contended, choose and apply a scheduling policy — priority assignment plus dispatching, e.g. FIFO, fixed-priority (semantic importance, deadline-monotonic, rate-monotonic), dynamic-priority (round-robin, EDF, least-slack-first), or static/cyclic-executive scheduling — matched to each resource's usage characteristics; in the energy realm, schedule work onto the most energy-efficient resources under task constraints.
elements.problem: Contention forces choices among competing criteria — optimal use, importance, latency, throughput, starvation-freedom — and the chosen policy determines which are met.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Substitution
aka: hardware substitution for software safety functions
elements.what: Replace potentially hazardous software design features with protection mechanisms — typically hardware devices such as watchdogs, monitors, and interlocks — that provide and control their own resources.
elements.problem: Software versions of protection mechanisms can be starved of resources by the very failures they guard against; substitution pays off when the protected function is relatively simple.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Comparison
elements.what: Detect potentially unsafe states by comparing the outputs of redundant components and flagging divergence.
elements.problem: A single component cannot detect its own erroneous output; comparison against redundant peers exposes it. Detection counterpart of the availability Voting tactic (which also chooses a result).
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Abort
elements.what: If an operation is determined to be unsafe, terminate it before it causes damage — the conceptually simplest way to make a system fail safely.
elements.problem: Continuing a hazardous operation converts a detected unsafe state into an accident; stopping is often the safest available response.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Masking
elements.what: Mask a fault by comparing the results of several redundant components and using a voting procedure when they differ, so the faulty result never propagates; requires a simple, highly reliable voter.
elements.problem: Some systems must keep producing correct outputs through component faults, not merely detect them; masking hides the fault behind redundancy.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Firewall
elements.what: A barrier that restricts access to designated resources (typically processors, memory, and network connections); a specific realization of the security Limit Access tactic used to keep unsafe effects from propagating.
elements.problem: Once part of a system misbehaves, unrestricted access lets the damage spread; a barrier confines it.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Interlock
elements.what: Protect against failures arising from incorrect event ordering by controlling all access to protected components, including enforcing the correct sequencing of events affecting them.
elements.problem: Some hazards arise not from wrong values but from right actions in the wrong order; an interlock makes illegal orderings impossible.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Repair State
elements.what: Repair an erroneous state — effectively enlarging the set of states the component handles competently — and continue execution, e.g. lane-keeping assist steering a drifting vehicle back between the lane lines.
elements.problem: Aborting or degrading is not always acceptable; some erroneous states can be actively corrected in place, though this is unsuited to recovering from unanticipated faults.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Detect Intrusion
elements.what: Compare network traffic or service request patterns within a system against a database of signatures or known patterns of malicious behavior (protocol, payload size, source/destination address, port).
elements.problem: Attacks in progress must be recognized among legitimate traffic before the system can react.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Detect Service Denial
elements.what: Compare the pattern or signature of incoming network traffic against historical profiles of known denial-of-service attacks.
elements.problem: Denial-of-service traffic must be distinguished from legitimate load spikes before countermeasures can be applied.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Verify Message Integrity
elements.what: Use checksums or hash values to verify the integrity of messages, resource files, deployment files, and configuration files, maintaining the redundant verification information separately.
elements.problem: Tampered or corrupted messages and artifacts must be detectable; even small changes must produce large, visible differences in the verification value.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Detect Message Delay
elements.what: Detect potential man-in-the-middle attacks by checking the time taken to deliver or receive messages against normally stable delivery times, and by watching for anomalous connect/disconnect counts.
elements.problem: An interceptor that reads or modifies messages in transit adds latency and connection churn that timing analysis can expose.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Identify Actors
elements.what: Identify the source of any external input to the system — users by user IDs; other systems by access codes, IP addresses, protocols, or ports.
elements.problem: Authentication and authorization presuppose knowing which actor an input claims to come from.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Authenticate Actors
elements.what: Ensure an actor actually is who or what it claims to be, via passwords, one-time passwords, digital certificates, two-factor authentication, biometrics, or CAPTCHA challenges, possibly with periodic re-authentication.
elements.problem: Identifiers can be claimed by anyone; proof of identity must back them before granting access.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Authorize Actors
elements.what: Ensure an authenticated actor has the rights to access and modify data or services, via access control mechanisms assigned per actor, actor class, or role.
elements.problem: Authenticated identity alone says nothing about what the actor may do; permissions must be checked per resource and operation.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Limit Access
elements.what: Restrict access to computing resources by limiting the number of access points and/or the types of traffic allowed through them — e.g. a demilitarized zone between internet and intranet bounded by a pair of firewalls.
elements.problem: Every access point and permitted traffic type enlarges the attack surface; minimizing both contains exposure.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Limit Exposure
elements.what: Minimize the damage a successful attack can do by reducing the amount of data or services reachable through any single access point — a passive defense that compartmentalizes value.
elements.problem: If one breached access point yields everything, every breach is catastrophic; spreading assets bounds per-attack loss.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Encrypt Data
elements.what: Apply encryption (symmetric or asymmetric) to stored data and to communication, providing confidentiality beyond authorization controls — and the sole protection on links that have none.
elements.problem: Data at rest and in transit can be read by parties outside the authorization perimeter; encryption makes possession without keys useless.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Separate Entities
elements.what: Limit the scope of an attack by separating entities — physical separation onto different servers/networks, virtual machines, air gaps, and keeping sensitive data apart from non-sensitive data.
elements.problem: Co-located entities share fate under attack; separation prevents access to one from becoming access to all.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Validate Input
elements.what: Sanitize and check input as it is received — filtering, canonicalization, and cleansing, typically via a security framework or validation classes — as an early line of defense.
elements.problem: Uninspected input is the vector for SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and kin; validation at the boundary stops malicious payloads before they reach interpreters.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Change Credential Settings
elements.what: Force users to change default security settings and credentials on delivered systems, and require periodic password changes.
elements.problem: Publicly known default credentials and stale passwords give attackers ready-made entry.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Revoke Access
elements.what: When an attack is believed to be underway, severely limit access to sensitive resources — even for normally legitimate users — until the threat is removed.
elements.problem: During an active compromise, normal access rights become an attack vector; temporary revocation trades usability for containment.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Restrict Login
elements.what: Limit access from a computer after repeated failed login attempts to an account, typically for a bounded period, sometimes doubling the lockout after each further failure.
elements.problem: Repeated failed logins signal credential-guessing attacks, but legitimate users also mistype; time-bounded lockouts balance the two.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Inform Actors
elements.what: When the system detects an attack, notify the relevant set of actors — operators, other personnel, or cooperating systems — so they can act.
elements.problem: An ongoing attack may require human or cross-system action that the detecting system cannot take alone.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Audit
elements.what: Record user and system actions and their effects so an attacker's actions can be traced and identified, supporting prosecution and improved future defenses.
elements.problem: After a successful attack, reconstruction of what happened and by whom is impossible without a maintained record.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Nonrepudiation
elements.what: Guarantee that the sender of a message cannot later deny sending it and the receiver cannot deny receiving it, via some combination of digital signatures and trusted third-party certification.
elements.problem: Transactions between mutually distrustful parties need binding evidence of send and receipt.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Specialized Interfaces
elements.what: Provide dedicated test interfaces — set/get methods for important variables, report methods returning full object state, reset methods forcing a given internal state, verbose/logging/instrumentation switches — clearly separated from functional interfaces so they can be removed.
elements.problem: Testers need to control and capture component state beyond normal inputs and outputs; but shipping code different from tested code is problematic in performance- and safety-critical systems.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Record/Playback
elements.what: Record information as it crosses interfaces and use the recorded state to 'play the system back', recreating the fault-inducing state as input to further tests.
elements.problem: The state that causes a failure is often hard to recreate manually; capturing it at interfaces makes failures reproducible, including in nondeterministic systems.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Localize State Storage
elements.what: Store system/subsystem/component state in a single place — conveniently a state machine object tracking and reporting the current state — so tests can start the system in any desired state, at whatever granularity testing needs.
elements.problem: Hidden or scattered state makes starting a test from an arbitrary known state difficult or impossible.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Abstract Data Sources
elements.what: Abstract the interfaces to a program's input data so test data can be substituted easily — e.g. repointing the system from a production customer database to test databases or data files without changing functional code.
elements.problem: Tests need controlled input data; hard-wired data sources force testing against uncontrollable production data.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Sandbox
elements.what: Isolate an instance of the system from the real world so it can be experimented on without permanent consequences, including virtualizing uncontrollable resources (system clock, memory, battery, network); stubs, mocks, and dependency injection are simple virtualization forms.
elements.problem: Testing against real resources with real consequences is dangerous or impossible (e.g. waiting for a real time boundary); a consequence-free, controllable replica removes the constraint.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Executable Assertions
elements.what: Hand-code assertions checking that data values satisfy specified constraints — placed wherever the data is referenced or modified, expressible as method pre/postconditions or class invariants — so the program flags when and where it enters a faulty state.
elements.problem: Faulty states can pass silently through execution; systematically placed assertions embed the test oracle in the code, increasing observability.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Limit Structural Complexity
elements.what: Keep the structure simple enough to test: avoid or resolve cyclic dependencies, isolate and encapsulate environmental dependencies, reduce inter-component coupling, constrain inheritance depth/fan-out and polymorphism, and track metrics such as response-of-class, propagation cost, and decoupling level.
elements.problem: Large operational state spaces make recreating an exact state — and thus reproducing failures — hard; high cohesion, loose coupling, and separation of concerns shrink the state space.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Limit Nondeterminism
elements.what: Find and, where possible, eliminate sources of behavioral nondeterminism such as unconstrained parallelism; where unavoidable (e.g. multithreaded response to unpredictable events), manage it with tactics like record/playback.
elements.problem: Nondeterministic systems are pernicious to test because failures do not reproduce; determinism restores repeatability.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Cancel
elements.what: Support user-issued cancellation: a listener not blocked by the operation being cancelled, termination of the activity, release of its resources, and notification of collaborating components so they act appropriately.
elements.problem: Users must be able to stop an in-progress operation; naive designs block the cancel path behind the very operation to be cancelled and leak its resources.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Undo
elements.what: Maintain sufficient information about earlier system state — snapshots/checkpoints or sets of reversible operations, with detailed change records where operations are not invertible — to restore it on user request, in single- or multi-level variants.
elements.problem: Users make mistakes; recovery requires the system to have planned for state restoration, since some operations (mass replace, or anything with external effects) cannot be reversed naively or at all.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Pause/Resume
elements.what: Let users pause and later resume long-running operations (e.g. large downloads), temporarily freeing resources for reallocation to other tasks.
elements.problem: Long-running operations monopolize resources and user attention; suspension without loss of progress restores control to the user.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Aggregate
elements.what: Provide the ability to aggregate lower-level objects into a group so an operation applies to the whole group, e.g. selecting all slide objects and setting one font size.
elements.problem: Repeating the same operation across many objects is tedious and error-prone for users.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Maintain Task Model
elements.what: Maintain a model of the task the user is performing so the system can infer context and assist — e.g. predictive type-ahead in search engines, spell correction in mail clients.
elements.problem: System-initiated help requires knowing what the user is trying to do; without a task model the system cannot anticipate.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Maintain User Model
elements.what: Maintain an explicit model of a user or user class — their knowledge of the system, expected response-time behavior, error patterns — updated dynamically or offline; user-interface customization is a special case where users edit the model directly.
elements.problem: One-size-fits-all interaction ignores what individual users know and need; encapsulating the model makes tailoring and modification easy.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Maintain System Model
elements.what: The system maintains an explicit model of itself to determine expected system behavior and give users appropriate feedback — the progress bar predicting time to completion is the canonical manifestation.
elements.problem: Users need feedback about what the system is doing and how long it will take; producing it requires the system to model its own behavior.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

rejected.name: ATAM (Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method)
rejected.why: Analysis/evaluation method, i.e. process, not an architecture element — excluded per charter rule.

rejected.name: Tactics-Based Questionnaires
rejected.why: Assessment instrument appearing in every bck QA chapter; process artifact, not an element.

rejected.name: Manage Work Requests
rejected.why: 4th-ed parent grouping whose two leaves (manage event arrival, manage sampling rate) are cataloged; the parent adds no distinct mechanism.

rejected.name: System Exceptions
rejected.why: Listed as a refinement of exception detection; names a category of processor exceptions, not a distinct tactic.

rejected.name: Function Patch / Class Patch / In-Service Software Upgrade (ISSU)
rejected.why: Named as realization variants of the Software Upgrade tactic; kept as aka.

rejected.name: Active Redundancy (hot spare) / Passive Redundancy (warm spare) / Cold Spare
rejected.why: 3rd-ed separate tactics merged in the 4th ed into one Redundant Spare tactic with hot/warm/cold variants; kept as aka.

rejected.name: Scheduling policies (FIFO, fixed-priority, semantic importance, rate-monotonic, deadline-monotonic, round-robin, EDF, least-slack-first, cyclic executive/static scheduling)
rejected.why: Named in a sidebar as policies selectable by the Schedule Resources tactic, not tactics themselves; the design realm already carries scheduling elements (e.g. dynamic-priority-scheduling) that will bridge here.

rejected.name: Component Replacement / Compile-time Parameterization / Aspects / Configuration-time Binding / Resource Files / Interpret Parameters / Shared Repositories / Polymorphism (as binding mechanisms)
rejected.why: Enumerated as binding-time mechanisms realizing Defer Binding (ch8) and as component-substitution techniques (ch12); realization-level, mostly covered by design-realm elements.

rejected.name: Preprocessor Macros (testability substitution technique)
rejected.why: ch12 lists it as a technique to swap in state-reporting code; a realization mechanism, not a tactic leaf.

rejected.name: Increase Cohesion / Reduce Coupling / Detect Faults / Recover from Faults / Prevent Faults / Detect Attacks / Resist Attacks / React to Attacks / Recover from Attacks / Containment / Limit Consequences / Barrier / Monitor Resources / Allocate Resources / Reduce Resource Demand / Control Resource Demand / Manage Resources (performance) / Limit Dependencies / Adapt / Coordinate / Control and Observe System State / Limit Complexity / Support User Initiative / Support System Initiative
rejected.why: Tactic-category headings, recorded as bck-cat: tags on the leaf elements instead of as elements — a catch-all node is worthless by mission rule.

rejected.name: Restore (security recover-from-attacks item)
rejected.why: ch11 explicitly delegates restoration to the ch4 availability recover-from-faults tactics rather than naming a distinct security tactic.

notes: Charter: full Bass-Clements-Kazman 4th-ed tactic trees (corpus id bck), chapters 4-13, all ten QA chapters. VERIFICATION: every tactic list verified live this session against the full text of Software Architecture in Practice 4th ed. via the chapter-by-chapter markdown mirror at github.com/suseme/arc_n_p (branch 4th-cn, docs/ch04.md-ch13.md; Chinese translation retaining the English tactic names), cross-checked with SEI blog posts ('Tactics and Patterns for Software Robustness', 'Two Categories of Architecture Patterns for Deployability') and search snippets of the O'Reilly edition. DEDUP: one element per tactic name across QA chapters with multiple qa: tags — timestamp, condition monitoring, sanity checking, predictive model, rollback, degradation, reconfiguration, timeout carry qa:availability+qa:safety; replication, functional redundancy, analytic redundancy likewise (ch4 voting refinements = ch10 redundancy sub-tactics); encapsulate, use an intermediary, abstract common services carry qa:integrability+qa:modifiability; discover carries qa:integrability+qa:energy-efficiency; schedule resources carries qa:performance+qa:energy-efficiency; the six ch9 control-resource-demand tactics also carry qa:energy-efficiency because ch6's Reduce Resource Demand category explicitly imports them. Deployment Rollback kept separate from availability Rollback (same name, different mechanism: redeploy-reversal vs runtime state reversal). SAME-NAME-TWO-REALMS: tagged same-name:design-realm on heartbeat, timeout, retry, rollback, self-test (design built-in-self-test), feature-toggle (design feature-flag), maintain-multiple-copies-of-data (design caching family), bound-queue-sizes (design bounded queue/backpressure kin), executable-assertions (design assertion kin), audit (design audit-log) — never collapsed; all ids suffixed -tactic for global uniqueness. HANDOFF TO PATTERN SCOUTS (met in these chapters, out of my tactics charter, NOT rejected as non-elements): microservices architecture, blue/green deployment, rolling upgrade, canary testing, A/B testing (ch5); sensor fusion, kill abnormal tasks, power monitor (ch6); service-oriented architecture, dynamic discovery (ch7); client-server, plug-in/microkernel, layered, publish-subscribe (ch8); service mesh, load balancer, throttling, map-reduce (ch9); redundant sensors, monitor-actuator, separated safety (ch10); intercepting validator, intrusion prevention system (ch11); dependency injection, strategy, intercepting filter (ch12); MVC, observer, memento (ch13). PROVENANCE NOTE for 3b: ch10 safety tactics derive from Wu & Kelly, 'Safety Tactics for Software Architecture Design' (COMPSAC 2004) — bck is the citable naming source used here; Wu-Kelly is an optional pass-8 addendum candidate if a primary naming citation is wanted. Element count 109: availability 32, deployability 6, energy 4 distinct (+shared), integrability 10, modifiability 4 distinct (+3 shared), performance 13, safety 7 distinct (+8 shared), security 18, testability 8, usability 7.
